name: Agentic Drafting and Multi-Model Workflows
title: Agentic Drafting and Multi-Model Workflows
answer: Agentic drafting and multi-model workflows describe a way of writing in which a language model is given a goal and a degree of autonomy, then allowed to plan, draft, revise and check its own output across several passes, often handing parts of the job to other models. In literary practice this covers outline generation, scene drafting, continuity checking, line editing and translation, with the writer setting the brief and judging the result. The unit of work is not a single prompt but a chain of steps, each with its own model, instructions and stopping condition. It sits alongside older drafting tools because the model is asked to act rather than only to answer.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These workflows run on hosted model APIs, local weights on a workstation, or a mix of both, joined by orchestration code that passes text, structured notes and files between steps. A typical chain uses one model for planning, another for prose, a third for critique, plus retrieval over the writer's own manuscripts, style guides and research notes. Memory is usually external, held in a project folder or database rather than in the model itself, so a long novel can be worked on in sections. Cost and latency scale with the number of calls, which is why many writers keep a cheap model for routine passes and a stronger one for final prose.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The writer defines the goal, the constraints and the voice, then breaks the work into stages such as premise, beat sheet, scene, revision and proof. Each stage has a prompt, an input, an expected output and a check, and the agent may loop until the check passes or a human intervenes. Multi-model routing sends a task to whichever model handles it best, for example a long-context model for continuity and a smaller one for dialogue polish. Human review points are placed where judgement matters most, typically at structure and final line level. Logs of prompts, outputs and edits make the process repeatable across a book or a series.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions turn on what went in and what comes out, so provenance records for training data, source manuscripts and model versions matter when a work is published or licensed. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, and any writer using these tools should expect the legal picture around generated text to keep shifting. Practical safeguards include keeping human authorship visible in the drafting record, checking contracts with publishers and agents about disclosure, and avoiding the ingestion of third-party manuscripts without permission. Style imitation of a living author raises separate concerns from generic pastiche, and both are usually handled by policy rather than by law alone.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect longer agent runs, better project memory and tighter integration with writing software, so a single session can carry a novel's continuity across hundreds of pages. Evaluation is likely to move from vibes to measurable checks on voice, fact and structure, which will make multi-model routing more deliberate. Rights and disclosure norms will harden as litigation resolves and publishers settle on standard clauses. The craft question stays the same: the writer decides what the book is, and the agent handles the parts of drafting that can be specified.
